query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys that start in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state, controlled thermal aging triggers the diffusion‐controlled nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds. When aging conditions are moderate, the resulting fine, uniformly distributed intermetallics support the development of a continuous, protective MgO-enriched passivating layer, thereby retaining or even enhancing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance. In contrast, under more aggressive thermal exposure, coarsening of these precipitates disrupts matrix continuity and the integrity of the protective oxide layer, leading to a degradation of these properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging treatments that simulate service-regime temperatures.
generation.conditions: A comparison between specimens aged under moderate conditions (expected to yield fine and uniformly dispersed intermetallic precipitates) and specimens aged under more aggressive thermal regimes (expected to produce coarser, discontinuous precipitates), with all tests conducted under similar oxidizing and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, distribution, and connectivity of the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that emerge from the metastable solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation drives the diffusion of Mg from the metastable matrix leading to nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. Under moderate conditions, fine precipitates form that promote a stable, continuous passivating oxide layer (e.g., MgO) which helps maintain corrosion and oxidation resistance. Under more aggressive conditions, excessive coarsening of precipitates disrupts the protective matrix and oxide film continuity, thereby impairing the alloy’s resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples aged under moderate conditions will develop a fine-scale, homogeneous intermetallic microstructure accompanied by retained or slightly improved corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state. Conversely, samples subjected to higher temperature or longer aging durations will exhibit coarser intermetallic precipitates, correlating with a measurable decline in corrosion and oxidation protection.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable solid-solution state, characterized by a homogeneous elemental distribution and initial protective properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within service regimes where thermal exposure is sufficient to initiate intermetallic formation (moderate aging) but below complete homogenization, with the transition to degraded performance occurring once aging conditions produce coarser, discontinuous precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative trends between fine versus coarse intermetallic evolution and the resulting protective properties are supported by reported behavior in Mg-containing alloys, the precise temperature and time thresholds for this transition remain to be determined and may vary with alloy composition and environmental factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare uniform samples of the Mg-containing high-entropy alloy in its initial metastable state. Subject one set to moderate thermal aging and another to more aggressive thermal aging (by varying temperature and duration) under identical oxidizing and corrosive conditions. Compare these with unaged control samples.
measurements: Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and connectivity
Surface analysis techniques (e.g., XRD, EDS) to characterize passivating oxide scale continuity and composition
Electrochemical tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) for corrosion resistance
Thermogravimetric or cyclic oxidation tests to evaluate high-temperature oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aging does not produce a clear correlation where moderate thermal exposure results in fine, uniform intermetallic precipitates and sustained or enhanced protective properties while aggressive aging yields coarse, discontinuous precipitates with a corresponding degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, thermal exposure within service regimes activates the segregation of Mg from the metastable solid solution, triggering the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. This phase transformation alters the alloy’s microstructural continuity—particularly along grain boundaries—thereby disrupting the uniformity of protective oxide layers and establishing microgalvanic sites that contribute to decreased corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium, single-phase solid solution of a Mg-containing high-entropy alloy.
drafts.intervention: Apply controlled thermal aging treatments representative of service-regime temperatures, with one set of samples aged while another serves as the room-temperature control.
drafts.conditions: Service environments that span from ambient to elevated temperatures near the activation energy for intermetallic precipitation (e.g., hundreds of hours of exposure) while subject to ambient oxidizing and corrosive atmospheres.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, particularly along grain boundaries and interdendritic regions.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal energy enables Mg atoms to segregate out of the metastable matrix and form intermetallic compounds. This process depletes Mg from the matrix—detrimental to passivation—and introduces heterogeneous microstructures that serve as microgalvanic cells. The resulting non-uniform distribution of phases disrupts the integrity of the protective oxide scales and accelerates localized corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-solid-solution (baseline) state, thermally aged samples will exhibit discernible, preferentially localized Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Corrosion testing (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation assessments (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis) will indicate a reduction in the stability and effectiveness of their protective films, thereby demonstrating compromised corrosion and oxidation resistance.
drafts.baseline: The initial uniform, metastable solid-solution state, where Mg is evenly distributed and contributes to maintaining passive film stability.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to be most relevant at the upper bound of the alloy's service temperature regime (temperatures and exposure durations sufficient to trigger appreciable intermetallic nucleation, e.g., hundreds of hours of aging near the onset temperature for precipitation) compared to ambient conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing high-entropy alloy samples. One set is maintained at room temperature to preserve the metastable solid solution, while the other is subjected to thermal aging at a temperature representative of its high-temperature service regime for a designated duration (e.g., hundreds of hours). Analyze both sets using microscopic (SEM/TEM with EDS), electrochemical (potentiodynamic polarization), and oxidation (thermogravimetric analysis) techniques.
measurements: Identify and quantify the presence, size, and distribution of intermetallic precipitates using SEM/TEM and compositional mapping (EDS).
Measure corrosion resistance via potentiodynamic polarization curves and determine variations in corrosion current density.
Assess high-temperature oxidation behavior by thermogravimetric analysis to evaluate changes in oxidation kinetics and mass gain.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after thermal aging, no significant formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds is observed or if the expected correlation between intermetallic precipitation and a decline in corrosion and oxidation resistance is not statistically significant compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the initially metastable solid-solution state seeds a transformation during service whereby controlled thermal activation leads to nucleation and growth of fine, Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds. When these precipitates evolve in a spatially uniform, submicron scale distribution, they assist in forming a coherent passivating layer (e.g., a MgO-rich scale) that preserves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance. However, when service conditions (temperature and duration) drive the intermetallic evolution toward coarse, isolated precipitates, the passivation network is disrupted, leading to diminished resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
drafts.intervention: Thermal aging and/or exposure to simulated service environments (e.g., high-temperature oxidation/corrosion testing) that provide sufficient thermal activation for intermetallic nucleation and growth.
drafts.conditions: A controlled comparison between specimens aged under moderate service conditions (predicted to yield fine, homogeneous intermetallic precipitation) and specimens aged under more aggressive conditions (predicted to produce coarse, agglomerated intermetallics), with all testing performed under otherwise identical environmental parameters.
drafts.structural_mediator: The distribution, size, and connectivity of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds that develop from the metastable state mediate the formation of a protective, passivating surface layer.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation during service induces nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds from the metastable solid solution. In moderate conditions, these intermetallics remain finely dispersed and promote a continuous passivating layer (e.g., via MgO formation), thereby preserving oxidation and corrosion resistance. In more aggressive thermal environments, the intermetallics coarsen and lose connectivity, which undermines the development of an effective passivating layer and leads to degradation in protective properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under moderate aging conditions, microstructural analysis will reveal a fine-scale, uniform dispersion of intermetallic precipitates along with sustained or even enhanced corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance. Under more aggressive conditions, coarse and irregular intermetallic formation will correlate with a measurable decline in the alloy’s protective behavior.
drafts.baseline: The initial, unaged state is characterized by a metastable solid-solution microstructure with no significant intermetallic precipitation and initial corrosion/oxidation resistance properties.
drafts.boundary: The relevant service regime boundaries are defined by temperature and time: conditions below a critical thermal activation threshold (e.g., moderate temperatures and shorter exposures) promote fine intermetallic formation, whereas conditions above this threshold (e.g., higher temperatures and/or longer exposures) drive coarse precipitate formation. (Exact temperature/time values remain to be determined.)

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare uniform samples of the Mg-containing HH-alloy and subject them to controlled thermal aging at two sets of conditions: (a) moderate temperature/short exposure (predicted to yield fine, homogeneous intermetallics) and (b) elevated temperature/longer exposure (predicted to yield coarse, discontinuous intermetallics). Perform microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to assess the spatial distribution and morphology of the precipitates and then evaluate the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance via standardized tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization for corrosion and cyclic oxidation tests).
measurements: Microstructural features (size, distribution, and connectivity of intermetallic precipitates)
Surface layer composition and continuity (e.g., observation of passivating MgO layer)
Oxidation kinetics and scale adherence from cyclic oxidation studies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the evolution from the metastable state does not correlate with the predicted change in intermetallic morphology (i.e., fine vs. coarse precipitates) and if no corresponding improvement (or degradation) in corrosion/oxidation resistance is observed when comparing the two aging regimes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Upon thermal exposure within service-relevant conditions, the metastable solid-solution Mg-containing high-entropy alloy undergoes a diffusion‐controlled transformation in which Mg partitions from the matrix to nucleate fine, Mg‐rich intermetallic phases. These precipitates, forming preferentially at grain boundaries and in the interior, mediate concurrent enhancements in high-temperature oxidation resistance (via more continuous, protective MgO‐rich surface layers) but provoke localized corrosion due to micro-galvanic coupling.
drafts.material_initial_state: A lightweight high-entropy alloy with Mg in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
drafts.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment simulating service temperatures (e.g., sustained exposure in the range of 500–700°C) to promote equilibrium transformations.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in an oxygen-containing atmosphere at high temperatures that mimic the service regime, with a controlled comparison between samples held at the elevated temperature and those maintained in the as-cast, metastable state.
drafts.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of fine, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form heterogeneously (especially along grain boundaries).
drafts.mechanism: Thermally activated Mg diffusion drives the partitioning from the metastable solid solution into Mg-rich clusters that evolve into intermetallic compounds. This transformation is kinetically limited so that, under intermediate exposure, the precipitates remain finely dispersed, enabling the formation of a stable, protective MgO-rich surface during oxidation. However, excessive intermetallic growth can disrupt the passivating matrix and create localized galvanic cells, accelerating corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, treated alloys will exhibit a dual behavior: improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (due to the formation of a more protective oxide scale linked to the Mg-rich precipitates) but a concomitant reduction in uniform corrosion resistance (as precipitate-induced galvanic sites enhance localized corrosion).
drafts.baseline: The untreated, metastable solid-solution alloy displays moderate oxidation resistance and relatively uniform corrosion properties owing to its homogeneous composition.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the service regime characterized by prolonged high-temperature exposures (500–700°C) with oxidizing environments; deviations in temperature, time, or environment (e.g., extremely aggressive corrosive media) might lead to different transformation kinetics or unstable intermediates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the Mg-containing high-entropy alloy: one retained in the as-cast metastable state and the other subjected to thermal treatment at 500–700°C for varying durations. Characterize the microstructural evolution using high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM, SEM) and phase analysis (e.g., XRD) to detect and quantify Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Simultaneously, perform high-temperature oxidation tests and localized corrosion measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) on both sets.
measurements: Protective oxide scale formation and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal treatment does not lead to measurable formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or if the evolution of oxidation resistance and corrosion behavior does not correlate with the predicted microstructural changes (i.e., either no improvement in oxidation resistance or no detectable increase in localized corrosion), then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Upon thermal exposure within service regimens, the metastable Mg-containing HEA transforms by nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that gradually deplete the protective alloying elements from the solid solution. This evolution alters the microstructural continuity required for an effective passivating oxide film, so that fine, evenly dispersed intermetallics (developed under moderate aging) may retain or even improve corrosion/high‐temperature oxidation resistance, whereas coarser precipitates (resulting from more advanced kinetics under higher thermal loads) lead to a loss of protection.
drafts.material_initial_state: A non‐equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state of a lightweight, Mg-containing high-entropy alloy.
drafts.intervention: Controlled thermal aging (annealing) at temperatures spanning the anticipated regime for transformation, with treatments at moderate and high temperatures to promote respectively fine and coarser intermetallic formation.
drafts.conditions: A service regime characterized by exposure to elevated temperatures that are high enough to activate diffusion (e.g., starting around 600°C) but below complete homogenization, with exposures long enough to trigger nucleation and coarsening phenomena.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation, distribution, and growth kinetics of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Thermally activated nucleation and growth wherein Mg segregates out of the solid solution to form discrete intermetallic phases. At moderate aging conditions, a fine dispersion of intermetallics maintains a relatively continuous matrix that supports the development of a protective passivating oxide layer, but at higher temperatures or longer exposures coarsening depletes the matrix of key elements, compromising oxide-film continuity and resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples aged under moderate conditions will exhibit a fine, dispersed intermetallic structure and either retained or slightly enhanced corrosion/high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state. In contrast, samples aged under more aggressive conditions will show coarser intermetallic precipitates, degraded passivation, and reduced corrosion/oxidation resistance.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, metastable solid solution showing homogeneous element distribution and initial corrosion/oxidation performance.
drafts.boundary: The transition between service regimes: below the threshold temperature/duration for significant intermetallic coarsening the resistance is maintained, while above this threshold the accumulation and growth of coarse precipitates degrade performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the Mg-containing HEA in its metastable solid-solution state and subject them to a series of isothermal aging treatments at progressively higher temperatures (e.g., 600°C, 700°C, 800°C) and controlled durations. Use identical samples as controls (i.e., unaged). After each treatment, perform microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, and EDS) to quantify the size and distribution of intermetallic precipitates and conduct standardized corrosion and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Precipitate size distribution and volume fraction via electron microscopy
Elemental mapping and phase identification (EDS, XRD)
Corrosion rate measurements (e.g., via electrochemical tests)
Oxidation resistance (mass gain/loss and scale morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in a systematic change in the intermetallic precipitate distribution (especially the transition from fine to coarse precipitates) correlated with a measurable change in corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state, or if improvements/declines in performance are observed independently of the predicted microstructural evolution, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis will be refuted.
